title: Straight Path
question: How does light travel through a uniform medium such as air?
choices: It does not travel at all
correctExplanation: Right. This straight-line travel is why shadows and sharp edges form.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is in straight lines. It is why a barrier casts a sharp shadow rather than a blurred pile of light.
lessonContent:
Straight paths create sharp shadows.
Obstacles block what travels in lines.
Observe edges to infer path shape.
Simple models explain many effects.
Share this: notice how a sharp shadow reveals the path of light.

title: Bouncing Off
question: When light reflects off a smooth mirror, how does the outgoing angle compare with the incoming one?
choices: The outgoing angle is always larger
The outgoing angle is always zero
correctExplanation: Right. The outgoing angle is measured from the same normal line and matches the incoming angle.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is they are equal. This predictable rule is what lets mirrors form images we can rely on.
lessonContent:
Reflection is symmetric about the normal.
Measure angles from the same reference.
Predictable rules allow precise design.
Use the pattern to trace light paths.
Share this: trace how a mirror redirects a torch beam.

title: Bending Light
question: Why does light bend when it passes from air into water?
correctExplanation: Right. A change of speed at the boundary makes the direction shift, which is why a straw looks broken in a glass.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it changes speed. The direction changes only at the boundary, not while travelling within one medium.
lessonContent:
Speed changes shift direction.
Bending happens at the boundary.
Everyday illusions follow from simple rules.
Observe carefully, then explain.
Share this: notice how an object looks bent in a full glass of water.

title: Bringing Together
question: Which lens shape can focus parallel light rays to a point?
correctExplanation: Right. Its outward-curving surfaces bend rays inward toward a focus.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a convex lens. The inward-bending shape concentrates light, which is why it magnifies and focuses.
lessonContent:
Shape determines how light bends.
Curved surfaces gather or spread rays.
Converging and diverging are opposites.
Link geometry to optical effect.
Share this: use a lens to focus sunlight and observe the bright spot.

title: Splitting White
question: What happens when a narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism?
correctExplanation: Right. Different colours bend by different amounts, so the beam fans into a spectrum.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it spreads into colours. White light is a mixture, and the prism separates its components by how much each bends.
lessonContent:
Mixtures can be separated by a property.
Different components bend differently.
A simple tool reveals hidden structure.
Connect observation to composition.
Share this: look for a rainbow formed by a glass edge or water spray.

title: Seeing Colour
question: What determines the colour an object appears to have?
correctExplanation: Right. We see the wavelengths a surface sends back to our eyes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the light it reflects. Change the lighting and the apparent colour changes with it.
lessonContent:
Perceived colour depends on what returns.
Absorbed light is not seen.
Objects do not glow with an inner hue.
Test colour under different lights.
Share this: compare one object's colour indoors and in daylight.

title: Dark Surface
question: Why does a black surface look black?
correctExplanation: Right. Little light returns to the eye, so the surface appears dark.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it absorbs most light. Absorption also explains why dark surfaces warm up faster in sunshine.
lessonContent:
What is absorbed cannot be seen.
Darkness follows from strong absorption.
Energy absorbed becomes heat.
Connect appearance to energy.
Share this: compare how two colours warm in the sun.

title: Bright Surface
question: Why does a white surface look bright in sunlight?
correctExplanation: Right. Most wavelengths bounce back, so the surface appears bright and colourless.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it reflects most light. High reflection is also why pale surfaces stay cooler in the sun.
lessonContent:
Brightness follows from reflection.
A surface can return almost everything.
Reflected energy does not become heat.
Relate appearance to energy balance.
Share this: notice which surfaces stay cool on a sunny day.

title: Coloured Filter
question: What does a red filter do to white light passing through it?
correctExplanation: Right. The filter absorbs other wavelengths and lets red through.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it transmits only red. Stacking filters removes more colours and can leave no light at all.
lessonContent:
Filters select by wavelength.
Absorption removes what does not pass.
Combining filters multiplies restrictions.
Predict which colours survive.
Share this: look through coloured materials at a light source.

title: Light Primaries
question: Which three colours combine additively to make white light?
correctExplanation: Right. Screens use these three because mixing them at full strength gives white.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is red, green, and blue. Pigment mixing follows different rules from mixing beams of light.
lessonContent:
Light and pigment mix differently.
Additive mixing brightens toward white.
Subtractive mixing darkens toward black.
Do not confuse the two systems.
Share this: examine the tiny dots on a screen with a magnifier.

title: All Primaries
question: What colour appears when the three additive primaries are mixed at full strength?
correctExplanation: Right. Combining red, green, and blue beams recreates the full daylight mix.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is white light. Adding light works opposite to adding pigments, which would darken toward black.
lessonContent:
Adding light increases brightness.
The three beams together give white.
Contrast with pigment behaviour.
Choose the system that matches the medium.
Share this: predict the result of overlapping coloured light beams.

title: Pigment Mix
question: What colour results from mixing all the usual paint pigments together?
correctExplanation: Right. Each pigment absorbs more wavelengths, so the mixture darkens and dulls.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a muddy dark shade. Subtractive mixing removes light, which is why pigments darken rather than brighten.
lessonContent:
Pigments subtract from the light.
More pigments mean more absorption.
Mixing paints darkens toward neutral.
Contrast with light mixing.
Share this: mix two paint colours and note how the brightness changes.

title: Opposite Colour
question: Which light colour is complementary to red, producing white when combined?
correctExplanation: Right. Cyan is the mixture of the other two primaries, so it completes red to white.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is cyan. Complementary pairs are found by combining the remaining primaries.
lessonContent:
Complements complete a mix to white.
Find them from the remaining primaries.
Colour wheels encode these relations.
Use pairs deliberately in design.
Share this: identify the complement of one colour you often use.

title: Blue Sky
question: Why does the daytime sky appear blue?
choices: The sun emits only blue light
correctExplanation: Right. Tiny air molecules scatter blue light across the sky more than red.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is short wavelengths scatter more. Scattered light reaches your eyes from every direction, making the whole dome look coloured.
lessonContent:
Small particles scatter some wavelengths more.
Scattered light arrives from all directions.
Colour can arise from scattering, not only pigment.
Connect physics to a familiar view.
Share this: explain one everyday colour by scattering.

title: Red Sunset
question: Why do sunsets look red?
choices: The sun cools in the evening
correctExplanation: Right. A longer path through the atmosphere scatters away the blue, leaving reds and oranges.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is light travels further through air. More scattering removes the shorter wavelengths before they reach your eyes.
lessonContent:
Path length changes what survives.
More travel means more scattering away.
The same cause explains blue days and red evenings.
Track how conditions alter an effect.
Share this: watch a sunset and describe the colour shift.

title: Rainbow Maker
question: What produces the colours of a rainbow?
correctExplanation: Right. Droplets bend and reflect sunlight, spreading it into its component colours.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is refraction inside water droplets. Airborne water acts like countless tiny prisms.
lessonContent:
Everyday objects can act as optical tools.
Droplets behave like prisms.
The observer's position matters.
Connect a sighting to its mechanism.
Share this: find how your position changes what you see in a rainbow.

title: Mirror Image
question: What kind of image does a flat mirror form?
choices: A virtual image behind the mirror
correctAnswer: A virtual image behind the mirror
correctExplanation: Right. The light appears to come from behind the glass, so no screen can capture the image.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a virtual image behind the mirror. Real images can be projected, while virtual ones cannot.
lessonContent:
Images can be real or virtual.
Virtual images cannot be caught on a screen.
Trace where light appears to come from.
Distinguish appearance from source.
Share this: compare a mirror image with one projected by a lens.

title: Spreading Rays
question: What does a concave lens do to parallel light rays?
choices: It focuses them to a point
correctExplanation: Right. Its inward-curving shape spreads rays apart, making objects look smaller.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it diverges them. This is the opposite effect to a convex lens, which gathers light together.
lessonContent:
Lens shapes have opposite effects.
Converging gathers; diverging spreads.
Choose the lens for the task.
Predict before you test.
Share this: predict the effect of one lens, then check it.

title: Magnifying Lens
question: Which everyday use relies on a convex lens?
correctExplanation: Right. The converging lens makes an object appear larger when held at the right distance.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a magnifying glass. The same shape also concentrates sunlight and is used in cameras and spectacles.
lessonContent:
One principle serves many devices.
Spot the shared component across uses.
Link a tool to its optical basis.
Recognise converging lenses in daily life.
Share this: find one more device that uses a converging lens.

title: Making Shadows
question: Why does an opaque object cast a shadow?
correctExplanation: Right. Light travels in straight lines, so an obstacle leaves a dark region behind it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it blocks the light. Transparent objects cast faint shadows because they let much of the light through.
lessonContent:
Blocking creates darkness.
Straight paths leave a clear gap.
Transparency affects shadow strength.
Relate shape to the object causing it.
Share this: compare shadows from clear and solid objects.

title: Darkest Shadow
question: What is the darkest central part of a shadow called?
correctExplanation: Right. This region receives no direct light at all, unlike the surrounding partial shade.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the umbra. The softer outer region, where light is partly blocked, is the penumbra.
lessonContent:
Shadows have internal structure.
Total and partial blocking differ.
Source size widens the partial region.
Examine edges to see the effect.
Share this: inspect the edge of a shadow cast by a lamp.

title: Soft Light
question: How does a translucent material affect light passing through it?
correctExplanation: Right. It lets light through while diffusing it, so objects behind appear blurred rather than clear.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is it scatters some light. Transparent materials transmit clearly, while opaque ones block entirely.
lessonContent:
Materials vary in how they pass light.
Clear, cloudy, and blocking are three cases.
Diffusion softens what is seen.
Classify by the effect on light.
Share this: compare three materials by looking through each.

title: Colour Detectors
question: Which cells in the human eye are responsible for detecting colour?
correctExplanation: Right. Cones come in types tuned to different wavelengths and work best in good light.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is cones. Rods are more sensitive to dim light but do not distinguish colour well.
lessonContent:
Sensors can be specialised.
Different cells suit different conditions.
Dim light trades colour for sensitivity.
Match the sensor to the signal.
Share this: notice how colour fades as light dims.

title: Speed of Light
question: Approximately how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
correctExplanation: Right. This enormous speed is the universal limit for transmitting information.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 300000 kilometres per second. The figure is why distant light still arrives almost instantly across everyday distances.
lessonContent:
Some constants anchor many calculations.
Speed sets a hard limit.
Huge numbers warrant a sanity check.
Remember one key constant.
Share this: estimate how far light travels in one second.

title: Why Colour
question: What property of light determines the colour we perceive?
correctExplanation: Right. Different wavelengths correspond to different perceived colours.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is its wavelength. Brightness changes intensity, while wavelength changes the hue itself.
lessonContent:
A physical quantity maps to a perception.
Separate intensity from quality.
Name the property behind an experience.
Use the right measure for the question.
Share this: distinguish brightness from colour in one lighting situation.
